finalText:
**Merge keeps both paths. Rebase makes one straight path.**

Merge ties the two branches together with one new commit. Your old commits stay exactly as they were.

Rebase copies your commits onto the tip of the other branch. Same changes, new commits, new IDs.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph after_merge
    A1[main] --> M[merge commit]
    B1[your branch] --> M
  end
  subgraph after_rebase
    A2[main] --> C1[your commit, copied] --> C2[your commit, copied]
  end
```

Reach for rebase on work only you have. It tidies messy commits before you share them.

Reach for merge when the branch is shared, or when you land a finished branch. The merge commit records when it joined.

One rule: never rebase commits someone else already pulled. Their copy and yours stop matching.

Because rebase writes new commits, pushing after one needs `git push --force-with-lease`.
